video_title: AI Is Changing Time: Those Who Can’t Compete, Compute
gist: Jordi Visser's weekly slide-driven macro/AI commentary argues compute demand is structurally insatiable and that AI agents are 'shrinking time' — producing 51% S&P earnings growth alongside the weakest six-month aggregate-payroll trend since 2012, a divergence he says invalidates academic/economist frameworks and the Fed's PCE-anchored hawkishness. He maps the capital flow into compute infrastructure (Apollo/BlackRock/Blackstone/Brookfield/Goldman/KKR half-trillion platform, Morgan Stanley $1.5T, Alphabet $25B, Intel $20B), argues Google is becoming the 'OPEC of compute' while losing frontier talent, and frames crypto rails/stablecoins as the next binding constraint once consumer agents arrive in 2027.

insights.claim: Compute demand should be modeled as structurally unbounded rather than cyclical, because each capability step-up (chatbots to coding agents to planning/reasoning agents to world models to humanoids) requires roughly another 10x compute, with no terminal state.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Treat compute-infrastructure exposure as a multi-year structural allocation, not a trade to fade on a single quarter's capex headline.
insights.quote: we are in a structurable market in the demand for compute. It is insatiable.

insights.claim: This year required 10-100x more compute for coding agents than last year's chatbot workloads, and the next two capability steps each imply another ~10x, which is the mechanical explanation for parabolic AI-infrastructure moves.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sizing compute TAM off current inference volumes understates it by an order of magnitude per capability generation.
insights.quote: So this year we needed 10 to 100 times for the coding agents relative to last year for chatbots. That's why everything went parabolic.

insights.claim: CoreWeave says A100 capacity introduced in 2020 is contracted out to 2029 and completely sold out, and useful-life assumptions for GPUs have moved from two-to-three years to six-to-nine years because supply of new data centers cannot replace old capacity.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Longer GPU useful life directly refutes the depreciation-fraud bear case and raises realized ROIC on installed fleets; watch other operators restating useful-life assumptions.
insights.quote: The A1 A100 is being contracted all the way to 2029. This was introduced in 2020. They're saying they're completely sold out.

insights.claim: Scarcity is so acute that buyers accept whatever hardware generation is available rather than waiting for the best one, meaning older GPU generations retain pricing power instead of being obsoleted.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Undermines the 'obsolescence risk' argument used against AI-infrastructure credit and asset values; legacy-fleet operators may be mispriced.
insights.quote: It's like walking into a supermarket. If they didn't have any food but cans of sardines, you would immediately love cans of sardines.

insights.claim: Reported data-center construction delays are net positive rather than a bearish signal, because memory supply is the binding constraint anyway and delays push committed revenue further out rather than cancelling it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fade headlines about data-center slippage as a bear catalyst; the contracted revenue is deferred, not lost, and memory remains the true bottleneck.
insights.quote: it doesn't really matter because we don't have enough memory anyway. So, all of these delays are actually good

themes.theme: Time Compression and the Earnings-Without-Hiring Anomaly

insights.claim: AI agents effectively compress calendar time because they work 24/7/365, so year-over-year comparisons are a human construct — a company now does roughly two years of work in one, heading toward three, four and five times.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes valuation: if the unit of time is compressing, historical y/y earnings multiples and cycle-length analogies systematically underestimate forward growth.
insights.quote: Agents don't sleep. Agents don't go to the bathroom. Agents don't go to lunch. Agents don't go to the pantry to flirt.

insights.claim: S&P 500 earnings growth of 51% with 15% year-over-year sales growth and roughly 47% global EPS growth proves the AI earnings boom is global and not an isolated bubble in a handful of US tech names.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The breadth of the EPS breakout (including the parabolic MSCI World Bank index) argues against a narrow-bubble framing and supports non-US and financials exposure.
insights.quote: You've got the whole globe breaking out in terms of earnings per share, and that's because time is changing.

insights.claim: The absence of hiring despite ~30-32% year-over-year S&P earnings growth is the key regime tell — historically firms threw more people at growing earnings, and the break in that relationship is evidence of AI-driven productivity, not late-cycle strength.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: This divergence is the single chart to monitor; it invalidates labor-market-strength arguments for Fed hikes and supports sustained margin expansion.
insights.quote: When I was at Morgan Stanley, if we had earnings growing rapidly, we'd be hiring people. That's what you did. You threw more money at more people. Not happening anymore.

insights.claim: Enterprise agents become persistent digital labor next year and consumer agents follow in the latter part of the year, meaning the deployment phase of coding agents has not even started yet.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If deployment is still ahead, current token consumption and compute revenue run-rates are an early-innings baseline, not a peak.

insights.claim: Private companies will capture much of the AI-driven earnings growth and 'steal from the public companies,' so public-market earnings can outpace prices without going parabolic.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues for private/pre-IPO AI exposure and tempers expectations that all AI value accrues to listed indices.

insights.claim: Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR are establishing AI compute infrastructure financing platforms to mobilize over half a trillion dollars of third-party capital, because Nvidia and hyperscalers no longer want to use their own balance sheets.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Confirms AI compute is being institutionalized as an investable asset class; alternative-asset managers are a levered proxy on the buildout.
insights.quote: AI factory computing investable asset class.

insights.claim: The capital for compute is demonstrably available: Morgan Stanley is facilitating a $1.5 trillion infrastructure initiative, Alphabet raised $25 billion in a week, and Intel's $15 billion stock offering was upsized to $20 billion with the stock trading above the issuance price.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Funding-availability is not the bottleneck; a financing-gap bear thesis is contradicted by successful oversubscribed raises, including Intel's re-rating.

insights.claim: US policy is actively subsidizing the buildout by exempting data-center bonds from key securitization rules, making it easier for data-center owners to sell asset-backed securities and opening the door to more debt issuance.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Regulatory tailwind for data-center ABS supply — watch spreads and issuance volume as a real-time gauge of buildout financing.

insights.claim: Frontier labs are willing to pay four to five times market pricing to secure large-scale compute, making them a concentrated buyer base whose revenue funds the vendor-financing loop with Nvidia — a circularity the speaker openly concedes rather than denies.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Brad Gerstner
insights.so_what: The 4-5x overpay is both the bull case (pricing power for compute owners) and the bear case (buyer concentration); monitor whether lab revenue keeps pace with prepay commitments.
insights.quote: It is circular. That's just the reality of what it is, guys.

insights.claim: Google's reorganization is best read as a capital-allocation shift toward selling compute rather than chasing AGI, because negative free cash flow is pressuring investors and infrastructure has guaranteed ROIC while model development does not.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If Alphabet's marginal dollar goes to infrastructure rather than frontier models, its multiple should converge toward an infrastructure landlord's, not a frontier lab's.
insights.quote: AI infrastructure may be the cleaner business than model development.

insights.claim: Google committed roughly $200 billion of capex this year to compute infrastructure earning a documented 30% ROIC that is tax-advantaged via accelerated depreciation with near-certain demand, versus model development requiring tens of billions with high variance and no guaranteed return.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A 30% documented ROIC on $200B of capex is the quantitative justification for hyperscaler spending — the number to attack or defend in any AI-capex bubble debate.

insights.claim: Talent departure from Google (Jeff Dean gone, Demis Hassabis predicted to possibly leave within a year) is a direct multiple-compression catalyst rather than a soft cultural story.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Treat frontier-lab talent flow as a hard valuation input for Alphabet; a Hassabis exit would be the trigger to re-rate Google as infrastructure, not intelligence.
insights.quote: if talents leaving, multiples compress. Plain and simple.

insights.claim: Companies that cannot compete on frontier models pivot to selling compute — the pattern Meta, xAI and Google are all following — and Google may win distribution and infrastructure economics while losing the model-prestige race.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, quoting 'Alex' via Moonshots podcast
insights.so_what: A clean sorting rule for AI equities: classify each name as frontier-model competitor or compute seller, and value each on the appropriate multiple.
insights.quote: Those who can't compete on the frontier models go towards compute.

insights.claim: Google is no longer the dream destination for top MIT-cohort builders, who now target OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and other frontier labs — the 'spiritual center' of AI has moved to private companies.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing 'Kush'
insights.so_what: Recruiting-preference data is a leading indicator of where AI value accrues; supports private-market AI exposure over incumbent large-cap platforms.
insights.quote: Google is no longer the dream destination.

insights.claim: The durable assets of scale for large companies are capital, physical infrastructure, distribution and regulatory position, so the rational endgame is the large company as capital allocator and infrastructure landlord to mission-driven vehicles it partly owns — firms that fight this by retaining everything internally will lose the talent and keep the costs.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A screening lens for mega-cap tech: reward those adopting the allocator/landlord model, discount those trying to hold every function in-house.
insights.quote: the rational endgame which Google is stumbling into or engineering is the large company as capital allocator and infrastructure landlord to an ecosystem of missiondriven vehicles

insights.claim: Elon Musk guided on SpaceX's first earnings call to 6-8 gigawatts of incremental data centers in 2027 alone and possibly well above 10 gigawatts, with semianalysis estimating SpaceX on track for about 10 gigawatts by year-end 2027.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing SemiAnalysis and Elon Musk
insights.so_what: Gigawatts are the new unit of value; SpaceX's buildout speed is a core part of its private valuation and a demand shock for power, memory and GPUs.
insights.quote: 6 to8 gawatts of incremental data centers in 2027 alone, possibly well above 10 gigs. Sounds impossible, but we believe it.

insights.claim: SpaceX has gone exclusive with Nvidia on Vera Rubin GPUs for orbital deployment while roughly 80% of its output is earmarked for space-based data centers, yet Musk is simultaneously building his own fab effort — a signal that memory, not logic, is the acute shortage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An exclusive Nvidia architecture commitment from the fastest data-center builder is a durable demand anchor; the parallel fab push flags memory as the next squeeze.
insights.quote: We think the Ver Rubin architecture is the best architecture. We're exclusive to Nvidia.

insights.claim: The correct positioning within the AI stack is to be long the receivers of capital — the infrastructure providers — rather than the hyperscalers deploying it, because Google's own talent loss proves even the best-capitalized players cannot get enough compute.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A clear side-selection rule: own the capital recipients (chips, power, data centers, memory) rather than the capex spenders.
insights.quote: I want to belong the receivers of the capital because the infrastructure demand is insatiable.

insights.claim: The next binding constraint on AI is financial rather than physical — consumer agents need settlement, stablecoins, tokenization and financial guardrails, making crypto infrastructure the 2027 bottleneck rather than compute.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Front-run the rotation from compute infrastructure to payment/settlement rails; this is the stated framework the speaker says to hold him accountable to in a year.
insights.quote: the next constraint is not physical, it's financial, the guard rails, consumer agents, the settlement, it's stable coins.

insights.claim: Figure's results are early proof of the tokenization shift: consumer loan marketplace volume was $4.3 billion, up 132% year-over-year, with tokenized on-chain marketplace Figure Connect now expected to approach 70% of volume.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A live, reported P&L datapoint for tokenized capital markets rather than a thesis — the 70%-of-volume migration rate is the metric to track quarterly.
insights.quote: We are building the modern capital marketplace amidst the paradigm shift in the capital markets towards tokenization and standardization.

insights.claim: Bot traffic will exceed human traffic by a factor of 1,000 within five years, making humans a rounding error on the internet and implying an explosion of machine-initiated transactions.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Elon Musk on Cloudflare's forecast
insights.so_what: If agent traffic is 1000x human, per-transaction infrastructure (payments, identity, verification, settlement) is the volume trade of the decade.
insights.quote: Humans will be rounding error on the internet. Bot traffic will exceed human traffic by a factor of 1,000 within five years.

insights.claim: Stablecoin card spending volume surged another 16% and a US bank regulator has opened national charters to Bitcoin and crypto firms, meaning crypto adoption is advancing regardless of whether the Clarity Act passes.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Do not position for a 'sell the news' event on crypto legislation; regulatory and volume progress is happening through the regulators, not Congress.
insights.quote: Just like AI, nothing stops crypto, guys.

insights.claim: Bitcoin should be viewed as the S&P 500 of the future — the index representation of the onchain economy — which is the organizing principle behind a 45-name, 10-vertical crypto ecosystem index the speaker has built and which is outperforming Bitcoin itself year-to-date.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Suggests equity-like crypto ecosystem baskets can generate alpha over spot Bitcoin during the adoption phase.
insights.quote: Bitcoin is a representation of the S&P 500 of the future.

insights.claim: AI and stablecoins could reshape rather than destroy dollar dominance, with a 'compute dollar' potentially replacing the petrodollar as compute evolves into an industrial resource, geopolitical asset and pillar of the monetary system.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Louis Gave
insights.so_what: A monetary-regime framing that links AI capex directly to dollar reserve status — bullish dollar-denominated compute assets and stablecoin rails simultaneously.
insights.quote: Gavka raises the provocative idea of a compute dollar replacing the petro dollar.

themes.theme: The Academic Fed vs Labor and Inflation Reality

insights.claim: The six-month rate of change in aggregate weekly payrolls — combining weekly hours, wage growth and hires — is at its weakest since 2012, a far broader measure than headline payrolls and evidence the labor market is contextually very weak.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: This is the speaker's claimed proprietary edge metric; if correct, the Fed hiking into 2012-level labor momentum is a policy error to position against.
insights.quote: we're at the weakest six-month rate of change since 12, 2012, 14 years ago

insights.claim: Non-farm payroll job creation is concentrated in healthcare and leisure — precisely the jobs AI cannot replace and the ones serving boomers with money — so ex-healthcare the labor market is already showing AI-driven job losses.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Headline payroll resilience is a composition artifact; strip healthcare and leisure and the AI displacement signal is already visible.

insights.claim: Wage data offers no support for hawkishness: average hourly earnings dropped to 3.2%, the Atlanta Fed wage tracker is at the same level as before 2020, and the quits rate is likewise back to pre-2020 levels while labor force participation keeps falling.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: No wage-price mechanism exists to justify hikes; positions for rate cuts or at minimum against a hiking cycle have a fundamental basis.
insights.quote: I don't see why the Fed should be raising rates especially not three times.

insights.claim: Core PCE is the single outlier among inflation gauges — Atlanta sticky CPI core 2.5, CPI core 2.6, Dallas trimmed mean 2.2-2.4 and Cleveland 2.7 average roughly 2.5 — and from 1990 to 2020 that average consistently ran above core PCE, meaning something has changed in the PCE calculation itself.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If PCE is structurally overstating inflation relative to its historical relationship, the Fed's primary metric is biasing policy hawkish — a mispricing in front-end rates.
insights.quote: only the PCE core, that one point is up there. Sounds like it's not a good one to use.

insights.claim: Kevin Warsh has implied core PCE could be jettisoned as the Fed's primary inflation metric as soon as January, and he speaks at Jackson Hole — a potential framework change markets have not priced.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Bill Dudley
insights.so_what: A change of inflation target metric would be a regime event for rates; Jackson Hole is the near-term catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: Worsh implied that the PCE index could be jettisoned as the Fed's primary inflation metric as soon as January.

insights.claim: The bond market's refusal to rally despite a downside inflation surprise, a retail sales miss and a prior-week jobs miss — with September odds now 31% for the Fed and 80% for the BOJ versus roughly 50/50 each before payrolls — is a market mistake rather than information.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Explicit call that the fixed-income market is mispricing; but he concedes the debasement trade needs yields to fall before it works.
insights.quote: Wall Street sees a bond market angst and we're seeing that the bond market just won't rally.

insights.claim: Sell-side research cannot cover the AI regime change because firms are built vertically in sector silos, and the same structure that makes a firm excellent at sector coverage makes it slow at cross-sector regime change — AI is not a sector, it spans industrials, materials, chemicals, energy, power and semiconductors.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Structural explanation for why consensus is late; creates a persistent information edge for cross-sector analysis of the AI trade.
insights.quote: The organizational structure that makes a firm excellent at sector coverage is the structure that makes it slow at a cross- sector regime change.

insights.claim: Academics and economists reliably lose money in a regime change because they ask what evidence says happened under comparable conditions, whereas markets ask what happens before everyone realizes and entrepreneurs ask what becomes newly possible.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An explicit filter for whose commentary to weight; he names Burry and Chanos as permabears who never update probabilistically.
insights.quote: Academics seldom change their view. That's what entrepreneurs do. That's what traders do.

themes.theme: Debasement Trade and Central Bank Gold

insights.claim: The debasement trade is only partially expressed — the dollar has already made new lows and gold and silver have moved, but Bitcoin has not yet responded, making it the lagging leg.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A specific catch-up trade setup: long Bitcoin against already-moved gold and silver, though he cautions it needs yields to fall first.
insights.quote: you should be buying the the basement trade. You should be buying gold, buying silver, buying Bitcoin.

insights.claim: Official-sector gold demand is re-accelerating: China added 20 tons in July, its largest monthly purchase since October 2023, is adding gold in Hong Kong, and the Bank of Korea has resumed gold investment after 13 years.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: New central bank entrants (Korea after 13 years) widen the official bid for gold beyond the usual buyers — a structural demand floor.

insights.claim: The US fiscal position is deteriorating faster than policymakers can grow out of it, and whatever the mechanism — yield curve control, raising the FIMA cap — Treasury is 'up against it' because spending is outrunning receipts.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Underpins the debasement trade: the policy reaction function to fiscal stress is monetary accommodation regardless of the specific tool chosen.
insights.quote: the debt and the deficit are just not getting better fast enough, even if they are getting better at all.

themes.theme: Tactical Risk Framework and Portfolio Evidence

insights.claim: The correct posture is structurally bullish on compute for three to five years while being tactically flexible on risk — reducing beta when risk/reward is poor and re-adding after panic and consolidation, without attempting to pick tops or bottoms.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Separates the structural thesis from the tactical trade — the only way to survive drawdowns in a parabolic secular trend.
insights.quote: on a structural basis I'm staying bullish the entire time. On a tactical basis it's shifting.

insights.claim: The speaker called 'parabolic exhaustion in memory' and was effectively out of everything including all Micron by May 17, then re-entered when Micron broke below 900, with the market since recovering more than 50% of the fall.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A documented, auditable tactical track record on the memory trade; the 900 level on Micron is his stated re-entry anchor.
insights.quote: I've been scaling out of things. I'm effectively as far as I'm concerned out of everything. Definitely out of all micron.

insights.claim: Concentration in AI names has massively outperformed the index: with NASDAQ up 20% year-to-date, the 100-name thematic portfolio is up 46%, the 25-name up 74% and the 10-name up 94% (equal-weighted 103%, median 65%), with the best up 249% and the worst — Nvidia — up 16.5% and still beating the S&P by 13%.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Quantifies that concentration, not breadth, has paid in the AI trade — average return roughly 7.9x the S&P's YTD return.

insights.claim: Despite being up 103% year-to-date, the 10-name AI portfolio has an average forward PEG ratio of 0.8 with median next-year earnings growth forecast at 40% and seven of the ten names expected to grow earnings over 30% — so the group is not expensive on growth-adjusted valuation.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A sub-1.0 forward PEG after a doubling is the core valuation rebuttal to bubble claims — the metric to check before trimming winners.
insights.quote: the average forward PEG ratio is 0.8. The median is 081. This is for the 10 names despite being up 103% year to date.

insights.claim: Market structure is showing tech momentum volatility elevated while NDX volatility barely budges — a dispersion signal that AI-driven earnings are compressing index-level risk even as single-name momentum risk rises.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Suggests hedging at the single-name/factor level rather than the index level, and points to dispersion trades.

insights.claim: Investors can build an unbiased sentiment tracker by feeding a chronological series of any commentator's weekly transcripts into an LLM prompt that scores long-term conviction, short-term outlook and willingness to take risk over time.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A directly replicable, low-cost method to audit any research provider's tactical accuracy rather than trusting recollection.
insights.quote: Go measure their tone.
